# Four kernel sizes, at the same time

Every convolutional network asks you a question it has no way to answer: **how big should
the window be?** A 3×3 sees fine detail. A 5×5 sees more context and costs nearly three
times as much. A 1×1 sees no neighbourhood at all and only mixes channels.

Inception's answer, from 2014, is to stop choosing. Run all of them on the same input, glue
the results together along the channel axis, and let training decide how much of each to
use by how much weight it puts on them downstream.

The graph is the idea. One tensor fans out into four paths, each looking at a different
scale, and a `Concat` gathers them back into one. The 1×1 convolutions in front of the 3×3
and 5×5 are not decoration — they **shrink the channel count first**, which is what stops a
5×5 over many channels from dominating the cost.

## Against a single-scale stack of the same shape

| network | parameters | validation |
|---|---|---|
| four parallel scales | **29,578** | **0.5715 ± 0.004** |
| one 3×3 stack, widened to match | 82,698 | 0.5555 ± 0.015 |

**Fewer parameters and a slightly better result.** The branching version uses 2.8× fewer
weights, which is the interesting part — the accuracy difference of 0.016 is close to the
control's own spread and should not be leaned on.

Where the parameter saving comes from is worth tracing. The single-scale control needs to be
wide to be expressive, and width in a 3×3 costs `in × out × 9`. The inception module gets
its expressiveness from **variety** rather than width, and three of its four branches are
either 1×1 or preceded by one. Cheap paths doing different jobs beat one expensive path
doing an averaged job.

This is the same argument the depthwise separable example makes from another direction:
**structure is cheaper than width.**
